items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1958-Fall
items.q: But when Handy showed you could make some money out of it, then everybody began to get it through.

ctx.x: Why shouldn't he tell the term of that? He's probably talking about Ammons and Johnson.

It might have been Ammons and Johnson, or Johnson and Turner. Who was it? There's a couple of them that were playing around New York. Yeah, they were around. Anyhow, the guys that only know one, too. That's what got it with Handy, too, you know. Because Handy hadn't really done something with it. The blues made plenty of money out of it. Johnny said, blues wasn't considered music in those days, which was a fact. They'd hush you up as you started playing it down there and go on and that kind of thing. And also, I…
You hear about the Bolden band playing ragtime. I wonder what they mean by that.

items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1964-11-28
items.q: Handy said, I had to sit back and watch this man direct my band.

ctx.x: claim in there but he said in there he said about the blues he said don't get me wrong i didn't he says i didn't invent the blue i didn't invent the blues he says but i've written many of them that's jelly said that see but he said don't get me wrong i of course general always kept a nice big dictionary beside him to check these words he sat right there at the head table down there with the dictionary and writing material on it and he did pretty well with it

That was what started it. Well, Handy himself, I think that your friend, Abby Niles, helped along with that little thing. What Handy did, in there he admitted he heard, for instance, what he called the Atlanta blues, which was Make Me a Pallet on the Floor or something like that. He admitted that he heard a Negro thumping it out on a guitar at a railroad station once, and he took out his pad and he put down the tune. See, he admitted that. And also he was interviewed by Dorothy Scarborough, which was a book about…
